newsitem.title: FRANCE: Legras says competition will help French farmers.
newsitem.headline: Legras says competition will help French farmers.

text.p: The EU's latest reform proposal is aimed at encouraging European farmers to compete on world markets as a basic principle, a senior European Union official said on Monday.

"The idea is to put European agriculture in a position to benefit from global growth. If there is a choice which favours French farmers then that is it," Guy Legras, the European Commission's director general for agriculture, said.
French farm unions have criticised the Commission's latest price-cutting proposals known as Agenda 2000, saying they would hit agricultural revenues.
Legras, on a one-day visit to Paris to explain the reform, told a news conference similar complaints against 1992 farm reform proved unfounded.
Since the reform was introduced, average farm household revenues had risen in Europe by four to 4.5 percent, with some variation according to sectors and regions involved.
Speaking in general terms about competitivity, Legras said French wheat, which is geared towards export, was already close to being competitive on the world market without subsidy.
"I believe that as far as wheat is concerned for example, France is already today practically competitive with the United States. The same is not true of maize," he said.
He said there was progress to be made in other sectors including beef.
Placating French farmers will be crucial in driving through the reform, which the Socialist-led government in Paris has criticised as a trade gift to the United States.
The plan outlined by European Commission President Jacques Santer last week calls for a 20 percent cut in cereals intervention prices.
Export refunds would remain in the EU's armoury but would not, if its calculations were correct, be needed, Legras said.

French wheat prices are currently around $20 a tonne above U.S. soft red winter prices, or $5 a tonne above hard red winter prices, but have fluctuated either side of world market levels during the past 18 months.
Legras said that besides boosting competitivity, the EU plan was designed to protect revenues and introduce new elements such as rural development into farm policy.

There would be some ceilings placed on EU agricultural aid, he said, but declined to give figures. Grain growers have resisted previous efforts to cap their income in the face of what the Commission describes as previous overpayments.

Legras said the sensitive question of "modulation" or variation between subsidies paid to different farmers would be included in the reform but this was being left to member states to carry out as they saw fit. --Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
